August 2009 # Red hot summer - Copper prices have had a blistering summer, averaging more than $5,100/t in July. Optimism about China and a renewed appetite for risk from investors have been driving the rise. However, prices are looking increasingly out of touch with fundamentals. CRU believes that a correction is likely. - Chinese demand has been robust, and we expect it to remain so in H2. However, a significant proportion of Chinese copper imports so far this year have built up as inventory and we believe optimism that current import levels can continue is misplaced. The world outside of China is experiencing very weak demand, with no major improvement expected over the balance of this year. - Mine supply has not cut back further and, with prices so high, there have been some reopenings. However, refined production growth is being constrained by low overall cathode demand and some smelters continuing to face problems disposing of acid. |The supply/demand

In July, the 3-month price rose steadily to hit a monthly high of $5,640/t on 28th

July. It then fell back to an official price of $5,421/t the following day, but this is still a rise of 6.3% since the end of June and an increase of 84.7% year-todate. Current prices lie some distance above what is supported by the fundamental cost structure of the industry. The price of copper has tracked the rise in stock markets, suggesting that much of the price rise is due to increased investor interest, as confidence builds and risk appetite returns. July‟s increases have also occurred on lower volumes, suggesting that a lack of sellers, rather than strong buying has boosted prices. From a fundamental perspective, it is tempting to point to strong Chinese imports as evidence of increased underlying demand, but consumption Copper prices have moved in

from developed nations still remains very weak. Although underlying consumption in China was up by 15.8% y-o-y in the first half, demand from the rest of the world fell by 22.8% y-o-y. Even though Chinese demand growth is very strong, supported by the country‟s stimulus package, it is still much weaker than headline imports figures suggest. CRU believes that a significant proportion of China‟s imported material is still being held as inventory in the country. We estimate that in the first half, of the net 371,000t build up in global off-warrant stocks (excluding the State Reserve Bureau and reported exchanges), about 90% (334,000t) was in China. Huge injections of liquidity into the Chinese market have attracted both domestic and overseas investors into copper. One major Chinese fabricator confirmed that there is a lot of speculation going on, explaining that for copper imported before May, inventories now have a paper profit and there would be no hurry to sell. The fundamentals suggest that prices should fall. So is a correction imminent then? Not for certain. Investor sentiment could continue to hold copper prices above $5,000/t for some time. Copper has taken on some of the lustre of gold, and it has become a favoured asset for the investment community. Prices have continued to climb in mid to late July, despite a net gain of 21,450t at LME warehouses since 13th July after declining for several months. Although market fundamentals will remain weak throughout the remainder of 2009, some Q2 economic figures are Forthcoming demand indicators likely to look good compared to the lows **Event Date** of Q1. News which shakes confidence in the economic or copper demand recovery could be the trigger for a marked reversal of trend. Given the importance of China to sentiment, perception as to that country‟s demand outlook will be central. The market‟s reaction to Chinese copper imports data for July, released in mid-August, will be a key one to watch. We expect imports to be lower than June‟s record high. If the fall is a large one, then the market reaction could be significant if exchange stocks have continued to build. ## **Chinese demand will ease in second half** After the precipitous decline in late 2008, over the last quarter global copper demand has stabilised at a low level, but a major recovery still seems some way off. Indeed, we expect that consumption volume in the second half of 2009 will be slightly less than in the first half. The second half of the year is normally the seasonally weaker period for demand in many countries. This year, summer shutdowns, a higher copper price and frontloading of consumption through government stimulus measures and procurement policies in many countries will exacerbate this trend. We also expect this second half slowdown in copper demand will be evident in China, due in part to lower wirerod production. However, demand will still remain fairly robust throughout the remainder of the year as the majority of stimulus money is still to be spent and further national grid expenditure is planned. In addition to infrastructure spending, copper will benefit this year from Chinese domestic consumption of copper in consumer appliances (supported by government initiatives) and better than expected demand for tube (boosted by a hot summer). Although the production of the majority of air conditioners and AC motors (used in appliances) was down in the first half, we beli

eve that some inventory has been run down which could help production in the rest of the year. 

Nevertheless, there are concerns over the China outlook.  At a wider economic level, although government spending has helped China offset the effects of weakening exports, there has not been any significant pickup in Chinese domestic consumer demand.  If export demand from developed countries does not pick up soon, China could see weakening demand for copper products ahead as stimulus options become exhausted. Lending growth could also slow as continued liquidity is likely to lead only to asset price inflation.  In addition, high prices and volatility mean that substitution remains a threat (in China and elsewhere, see Consumption Trends section, p. 8-9). 

The reliance of the Chinese market on domestically generated demand is shown in recent analysis we have undertaken on semis trade.  This shows that unlike last year, Chinese semi-fabricated copper products production has not been boosted by export growth and replacement of semis imports.  On current trend, net imports for 2009 of copper semis and wire and cable look set to remain at the same level as last year.  This is in contrast to 2008 when falling semis imports and rising exports boosted Chinese copper consumption by 172,000t. 

In the developed world, there is still some way to go to overcome current economic problems. Unemployment rates are rising, as are default rates on credit cards, mortgages and business lending.  Some markets, such as construction, are unlikely to see a rapid recovery.  Scrappage schemes to encourage automotive consumption may have „borrowed‟ consumption from the future, only delaying further restructuring and recovery. 

CRU believes that the recovery that is currently being priced in is too robust.  Chinese consumption is strong but is not as substantial as import levels might suggest.  Globally, credit is still tight and expensive for consumers and for all but the largest businesses.  Furthermore, the re-stocking effect of the recovery on enduse copper demand is likely to be more muted than some hope.  In a serious economic downturn such as is

## **Smelters feeling the pain** 

Smelters and refineries continue to suffer from a combination of poor raw materials supply, excess capacity and difficulties disposing of sulphuric acid.  Demand remains weak and several Japanese smelters have recently stated that they will continue with production cuts throughout 2009.  Sumitomo intends to maintain its production cuts throughout the second half of the year.  The company anticipates slowing consumption from China, and said it did not export any copper to the country in June due to weak

er demand. Mitsubishi Materials had hoped to return to normal production in October, but now says that it looks unlikely that Japanese domestic demand will recover sufficiently for it to do so. ## **Elevated prices lead to some reopening of mines…** Mine production has seen no further cutbacks in recent months due to the high price, and indeed there have been some re-openings. Scrap supply has also improved slightly in recent months due to higher prices, but generation rates remain low as the main suppliers of scrap for the developing world are all in the developed world. Scrap discounts are reported to have widened recently, suggesting the market is becoming less tight. Recent disruptions may have supported the bullish price sentiment, but have had relatively little impact on production. The most significant upset has been the breakdown of the conveyor belt at Collahuasi. However, current indications are that the impact on output is unlikely to be more than around 20,000t. ## **… but mine costs still high by historical standards** Relationship between price and stocks:consumption potentially shifting to a higher trend The average cost of producing copper, which provides the fundamental floor for prices, has fallen significantly from its 2008 peak. But in 2009, according to CRU‟s mine cost model, mine costs remain about 50% above the 2003 level due to higher price levels for many mine inputs. Almost all input costs have seen a rise in real terms, and some of these are unlikely to rapidly reverse, particularly given low inflation. Labour costs and royalties have both risen, as have consumable costs (such as oil) and power. As a result of this shift in costs, the relationship between the stocks:consumption ratio and price has shifted upwards, as shown in the accompanying chart. Even though we expect prices to fall, they are unlikely to fall to levels below $1.50/lb even if stocks rise significantly. 400

In absolute terms, the price differential has fallen dramatically along with the level of copper prices, as the first chart illustrates. The most recent quarterly peak differential was achieved in Q2 2008, at over $5,500/t. Copper fell faster than aluminium late last year and early this, narrowing the gap to a little over $2,000/t. In Q2 the gap widened to over $3,000/t, as copper prices leapt towards $5,000/t. While important, the absolute differential is not the only consideration in making substitution decisions. In previous research, CRU identified that the ratio of the price of copper to competing materials is another significant issue. Aluminium is the most frequent substitute for copper and we have identified a ratio above 3:1 as a trigger level to drive substitution. In Q2 2009 the ratio rose to 3.14, above the recent high of 3.09 hit in Q3 2006 (see second chart at right). In terms of tonnage, copper faces one of its biggest threats in the utility power cable sector. Alcoa recently

reported that it has been very successful in supplying aluminium to this sector rather than copper. China in particular is using aluminium for its utility power cables instead of copper. In the case of air conditioner tube, technical specifications are relatively more important, especially in light of regulatory requirements for increased energy efficiency. However, cutbacks in expenditure in the recession mean that research and development budgets have been slashed, which has slowed development work towards using aluminium rather than copper. Finally, the ongoing shifts away from copper are continuing in the plumbing and telecoms sectors, which are long-term, irreversible trends. © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 8 of 12 Copper Monitor August 2009 www.crumonitor.com Another key consideration regarding substitution is managing price volatility. In this as well, copper has been at a disadvantage since prices began to rise in 2003. In the early 2000s changes in the price of copper and aluminium were confined to a relatively narrow band of less than ±10%. With the China effect and the rise in metals prices, copper began to experience both higher prices and higher price volatility than aluminium. The narrow band at the beginning of the decade quickly expanded to one of ±30% for copper but only ±15% or so for aluminium, as demonstrated in the accompanying chart. This higher volatility continued into 2009 and is likely to continue over H2, as copper prices are likely to come under pressure. s|e mont|hs, seas|onally| © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 9 of 12 Copper Monitor August 2009 **www.crumonitor.com** # Industry News ## **Production** - On 8th July, an arson attack on a road leading to **Freeport-McMoran Copper & Gold’s Grasberg** mine in Indonesia set a bus shelter and security post alight. Mine operator **PT Freeport Indonesia** announced that no one had been injured and mining operations were able to continue as normal since the fire location was some distance from the mine itself. On 13th July, it was reported that an Australian construction manager and a Freeport security guard were shot dead in separate incidents near the mine. A number of policemen and security personnel have also been wounded in these and other attacks, but mining operations have continued as normal. It was later reported that 12 people, including two workers at Grasberg, have been detained by police in relation to the attacks. In 2009, Grasberg is expected to produce 691,000t of copper in concentrate. - It was announced on 22nd July that there is an electrical problem with one of the main conveyor belts at **Collahuasi** in Chile. The main conveyor belt is 7km long and delivers ore from the open pits to a 400,000t capacity stockpile, which then feeds into the adjacent concentrator via a smaller conveyor belt. The company said it will lose 5% of this year‟s production and that the repairs will take place in the next two months. Prior to this disruption, CRU had expected Collahuasi to produce 425,000t of copper in concentrate in 2009, and 59,000t of SXEW copper cathodes. - Indonesia‟s government and **PT Newmont Nusa Tenggara** (NNT) agreed on 16th July to value NNT at US$3.52B, after an earlier valuation by **Newmont Mining** of US$4.9B was rejected by the government. NNT, a subsidiary of Newmont Mining, **Sumitomo Corp** and **PT Pukuafu Indah** , operates the **Batu Hijau** copper-gold mine. The valuation now allows the disinvestment of a portion of Newmont and Sumitomo‟s interest in the company to go ahead, with the Indonesian government having the first right of refusal. Batu Hijau will produce 207,000t of copper in concentrate in 2009. - In July, attempts to forge an agreement over the ownership of **Invanhoe Mines Ltd’s Oyu Tolgoi** project have continued, with Mongolia‟s government voting to allow approval discussions to move to the next stage – the first official reading of the proposed investment agreement before parliament. According to reports, **Rio Tinto** (which owns a 9.95% stake in Ivanhoe Mines Ltd) said that the government would have had the right to a 34% stake in the project under an agreement drafted in 2007. However, talks failed at that time, and in the last month

there have been reports that Mongolia‟s president wants the country to take a share in profits, rather than an equity stake.  The Oyu Tolgoi deposit is one of the largest copper ore resources in the world and CRU expects it to produce some 360,000t/y of copper in concentrates, with start up not expected before 2013. 

- **Jiangxi Copper Corporation** announced in early July the completion of the first stage of their expansion of the **Dexing** copper mine, which increased ore production by 7,500t/d.  Over the next 18 months the capacity of the operation is to increase from 100,000t/d of ore to 130,000t/d, as Jiangxi Copper aims to reduce its dependency on imported copper concentrates for its smelters.  The resulting increase in copper output is expected to be 160,000t/y, up from the current figure of 120,000t/y.  Dexing copper mine, situated in Jianxi province, is the largest copper mine in China. 

- On 9<sup>th</sup> July it was reported that **China Metallurgical Group Corp** (CMGC) has begun construction work on the **Aynak** project in Afghanistan, after numerous delays caused by security concerns and the need to remove landmines and fill in bomb craters around the site. - **PanAust** shareholder approval was issued on 8<sup>th</sup> July for the acquisition of 19.9% of the Australian miner by **Guangdong Rising Assets Management Company Limited** . For the deal to go through, all that remains is Chinese regulatory approval, after approval from the Foreign Investment Review Board of Australia was given in late June.  The total investment, to be completed in stages, amounts to US$175M (A$216M). 

- The Foreign Investment Review Board of Australia approved on 8<sup>th</sup> July the acquisition of  a 19.9% stake in Australian miner **Kagara Ltd** by Chinese company **GFTG Shengtuo Metals** , and on 16<sup>th</sup> July Kagara announced the completion of the deal, worth US$46M (A$57M). 

- On 3<sup>rd</sup> July, **Teck** announced that **China Investment Corporation** (CIC) had agreed to purchase 101.3 million Class B voting shares in Teck, which represents roughly 17.2% equity and a 6.7% voting interest in the company.  CIC‟s investment, amounting to US$1.36B (C$1.745B), is being made through a wholly owned subsidiary company, **Fullbloom Investment Corporation** . 

- It was announced on 7<sup>th</sup> July that the failed SAG mill at **Golden Grove** copper-gold-zinc mine is now back online, after suffering a mechanical failure on 12<sup>t

h</sup> June, which prompted a shutdown. Golden Grove is one of the assets that **OZ Minerals** has sold to **China Minmetals Group** , and it is now operated by **Minerals and Metals Group** , which was formed to manage the assets. 

## **Exploration and Development** 



- A bill proposing that **Codelco** uses US$1.0B of their 2008 profits to fund project development activities has passed committee review and been approved for debate on the floor of Chile‟s senate. The company intends to raise a further US$1.0B for the same purpose through borrowing.  The bill also contains proposals to alter the structure of **Codelco** ‟s board of directors, with the aim of improving efficiency within the company. 

## **Smelting and Refining** 







- It has been reported that agreements over treating and refining charges (TC/RCs) for the year starting in July have been reached between **BHP Billiton** and the Japanese smelters.  According to press reports, fees are 33% down from contracts for January – December and set at US$50/t or cUS$5/lb. 

- The Chinese government has scrapped the 5% tax on sulphuric acid exports, starting from 1<sup>st</sup> July 2009, in an apparent move to assist smelters in finding an outlet for their acid.  Separately, in another indication of the current difficulties faced by smelters, the Ministry of Commerce has appointed the Chinese Non-Ferrous Metals Industry Association to conduct an anti-dumping investigation into sulphuric acid imports from Japanese and South Korean smelters.  There has so far been no comment from the Japanese and South Korean smelters concerned. 

- **KGHM** announced they had entered into a purchase-sale contract with **Salobo Metals** of Brazil (a subsidiary of **Vale** ) to purchase copper concentrates from the **Salobo** mine between 2012 and 2016, with an option to extend the agreement for a further 5 years.  The contract is worth between US$639M and US$969M over the 5 year period.

## **Consumption** 









- According to data released by the **Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association** , copper wire and cable shipments in Japan rose by almost 20% m-o-m in June to an estimated 53,600t.  But on a y-o-y basis shipments were down by nearly 25%.  Market participants commented that it is too early to speak of a recovery.  However, some improvement from the semiconductor and automobile sectors was evident.  Also, the **Japan Copper and Brass Association** announced that production of rolled copper semis in June rose by 18% m-o-m to 56,775t on a seasonally adjusted basis.  Even though the figure was down 30% y-o-y, it was the third sequential monthly increase. 

- **Belden** said that it is planning to cease production at one of its **Massachusetts** facilities.  The plant makes wire and cable products for enterprise applications throughout the **US** .  Production will m

ove to other existing plants of the company in **Leominster, Massachusetts, Monticello, Kentucky,** and **Nogales, Mexico** .  The decision of the company will result in 170 job losses. 

- Copper wirerod output of **Hindalco’s** subsidiary **Birla Copper** in **India** reached 145,542t in the FY ended 31 March 2009, a 4.2% increase compared with the previous fiscal year.  In Q4 FY 2009 the company manufactured 41,347t of copper wirerod.  This represented a 15.6% y-o-y growth. 

- **Nexans** , the **French** cable giant, published consolidated financial statements for H1 2009.  Sales for the first six months of 2009 reached EUR2,514 million (US$3,587 million) or EUR2,085 million (US$2,975 million) at constant metal prices.  Including the contribution of the acquired companies **Madeco** and **Intercond** , sales fell by 12.1% y-o-y.  The cable business alone declined by 16.4% y-oy, mainly due to the slowdown experienced in **North America** and **Europe** .  But the 1.7% q-o-q rise in Q2 reflected that the situation had stabilised.  In H1 2009 the group suffered a net loss of EUR57 million (US$81 million) primarily attributed to exceptional items.  Furthermore, Nexans announced the signature of an agreement to sell its copper wirerod mill business in **Montreal, Canada** .  The transaction, for which closing is expected in the third quarter of 2009, is subject to a certain number of conditions and the approval of the relevant regulatory authorities.
